title: 'We Cannot Remain Helpless Spectators': Jaishankar Presses Dialogue as Wars Hit Distant Economies
excerpt: At a UN Day address in New Delhi, the external affairs minister urged the UN to show leadership, renewed India's call for Security Council reform, and described a 4F crisis of finance, fuel, food and fertiliser facing the Global South.
body:
• External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar told a UN Day gathering in New Delhi on Sunday that the world "cannot remain helpless spectators" as the wars in Ukraine and West Asia impose costs on countries far from the fighting.
  • He said India speaks for global sentiment in urging that dialogue and diplomacy are the only solution, and that India is making its own efforts and is open to working with partners.
  • Jaishankar renewed India's call for reformed multilateralism, saying large parts of the world, especially the Global South, cannot be left out of decision-making.
  • He described the Global South as facing a "4F crisis" of finance, fuel, food and fertiliser, and called terrorism used as an instrument of statecraft "simply unacceptable."

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar on Sunday said the world cannot stand by while the wars in Ukraine and West Asia raise costs for societies that had no part in starting them. Speaking at the Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav Global Sammelan at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on the occasion of UN Day, he urged the United Nations to show leadership rather than watch global crises unfold.

"There are today two major conflicts going on in the world: in Ukraine and in West Asia or the Middle East. Societies and economies, peoples far away, who have little say in the matter, are actually paying the cost. We cannot remain helpless spectators," Jaishankar said, according to ANI reporting carried by New Kerala.

"We cannot remain helpless spectators."

— S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister

Dialogue and diplomacy as India's stated position

Jaishankar said India's position reflects a wider global view. "India expresses global sentiment when we urge that dialogue and diplomacy are the only solution. We are making efforts ourselves and are open to working with other partners to that end," he said. The remarks restate the line New Delhi has held since the Ukraine war began: the conflict will not be settled on the battlefield, and India will talk to both sides.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=-BAk3V2sP-8

He framed the speech around the founding choice made eight decades ago, when the world emerged from the Second World War and chose cooperation in creating the United Nations. UN Day, he said, is a reminder of that spirit of oneness, and of the UN Charter's aim of harmonising the actions of nations toward common goals. Whether the challenge is war, economic disruption or development, he argued, it can be addressed most effectively collectively.

A direct case for UN reform

The minister used the address to press India's long-running demand for an overhaul of global decision-making, including the UN Security Council. "We live in an imperfect world, but we all continuously strive towards greater perfection. Where the UN is concerned, that means recognising its shortcomings and limitations, and seeking its improvement. The case for reformed multilateralism gets stronger by the day. Large parts of the world cannot be left out of decision-making," he said.

"The UN must show leadership, not be a spectator to global crises," he added, in remarks reported by the Times of India. India has argued for years that a Security Council still shaped by the settlement of 1945 does not reflect today's distribution of population, economic weight or peacekeeping contributions, and that the Global South is systematically under-represented.

Terrorism and the Global South's 4F crisis

Jaishankar also described terrorism as a major threat to global peace and rejected its use as a policy tool. "Its usage as an instrument of statecraft is simply unacceptable. It can never be justified, it can never be rationalized," he said, adding that some countries continue to let political calculations take precedence over the fight against terrorism despite the lessons of history.

On the economic fallout, he said developing countries face a "4F crisis" spanning finance, fuel, food and fertiliser. Developed countries, he argued, also have a stake in finding solutions, and he called for urgent steps to reduce risks in the international economy and give nations more diversified options. "Market distortions through constriction and choke points only add to suffering. A genuine dialogue in this regard is overdue," he said.

Why it matters beyond New Delhi

The costs Jaishankar described are concrete for households far from either war: fuel and food prices set in global markets, fertiliser costs that feed into farm economies, and shipping choke points that raise the price of traded goods. For the Indian diaspora, those pressures arrive as higher energy bills and grocery costs in the countries where they live, at the same time as families in India absorb the same inflation through a different currency.

What to watch

India's reform push now runs through every major multilateral forum it joins, and New Delhi will carry the same argument into upcoming UN and G20 engagements. The test of the speech is whether the call for dialogue produces new Indian mediation efforts on Ukraine or West Asia, and whether the Security Council reform debate moves beyond the annual round of statements. For now, Jaishankar has set out India's position in its clearest form: the wars are everyone's economic problem, and spectatorship is not a policy.
